To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

there is no clear evidence that exposure of the fetus to maternal smoking is related to the risk factors for cardiovascular diseases in adulthood, after controlling for the effects of lifestyle in early adulthood.
there is an association between maternal smoking and lower levels of HDL cholesterol in early adulthood.
maternal smoking during the pregnancy is associated with a lower HDL cholesterol level in adulthood, after controlling for perinatal factors, adult behavioral factors and adult anthropometry.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of smoking during pregnancy on cardiovascular risk factors.
the effects of prenatal and early postnatal exposures on later health.
the effects of maternal smoking during the prenatal period on the metabolic cardiovascular risk factors among the adult children of the 1982 birth cohort of Pelotas.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effect of prenatal smoking on metabolic cardiovascular risk factor in adulthood is likely negligible.
there is no evidence of an effect of maternal smoking on cardiovascular risk factors in adulthood.
maternal smoking during gestation does not have any effect on metabolic cardiovascular risk factor levels among adults.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there is no evidence that maternal smoking during gestation is associated with cardiovascular disease risk factors in early life.

the effects of maternal smoking on cardiovascular risk factors in adulthood are not mediated by perinatal factors, and the effect on HDL cholesterol is not mediated by lifestyle variables in adulthood.
maternal smoking during gestation does not seem to program offspring metabolic cardiovascular risk.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is no clear evidence that maternal smoking during the pregnancy programs cardiovascular risk in adulthood.
the effects of maternal smoking during gestation on metabolic cardiovascular risk factor are likely due to confounding factors, such as lifestyle patterns, and not to a direct programming effect.
there is no evidence that prenatal exposure to tobacco smoke is associated with metabolic risk factors for cardiovascular diseases in young adulthood.
